# Configuration

Every option is optional. The smallest setup is one entry in `plugins`:

```json
{
  "plugins": [{ "package": "github:joe-broadhead/opencode-notion#v0.0.1" }]
}
```

To set options, use the object form:

```json
{
  "plugins": [{ "package": "github:joe-broadhead/opencode-notion#v0.0.1", "options": { "allowUntestedHost": true } }]
}
```

## Options

Set options with the object form of the plugin entry:

```json
{
  "plugins": [{ "package": "github:joe-broadhead/opencode-notion#v0.0.1", "options": { "access": "ask-changes" } }]
}
```

### `access`

- Type: `"all"`, `"ask-changes"` or `"read-only"`.
- Default: `"all"`.

How much the default rules restrict. `all` allows every Notion tool; `ask-changes` allows a read and asks for every other
tool; `read-only` allows a read and denies every other tool, which also hides it from the model. The classes come from
`src/notion-tools.ts`, so the value decides a tool Notion adds later too. [Permissions](#permissions) has the three
generated blocks.

### `allowUntestedHost`

- Type: `true` or `false`.
- Default: `false`.

The plugin supports OpenCode `>=2.2.3 <2.3.0`, the range `opencode.host` in `package.json` declares, and every check runs
on 2.2.3, 2.2.4, 2.2.5 and 2.2.6, the tested releases. Status shows the version, whether it is tested and the supported range in
its `OpenCode` row, for example `2.2.5 (tested; supported range >=2.2.3 <2.3.0)`.

- **A tested release:** the plugin starts.
- **Another release inside the range, such as 2.2.99:** the plugin starts too. Status marks the version `untested`, and the
  status RPC's `host.tested` is `false`. The next step is the same as on a tested release.
- **Outside the range, including 2.3.0, prereleases and development builds:** the plugin refuses to start, and `/plugins`
  shows:

  ```text
  HOST_UNTESTED: This plugin supports OpenCode >=2.2.3 <2.3.0, found 2.3.0. Next step: Use OpenCode >=2.2.3 <2.3.0, or set the plugin option "allowUntestedHost": true to run anyway.
  ```

- **Outside the range with `"allowUntestedHost": true`:** it starts anyway, and `/notion-status` and `/notion` show a
  warning.

There is no other option. To narrow what the model may do in Notion per agent or per tool, use permission rules; see
[Permissions](#permissions).

## Your own `mcp.servers.notion`

If your config defines no server named `notion`, the plugin registers one:

```json
{ "type": "remote", "url": "https://mcp.notion.com/mcp", "oauth": { "scope": "default" } }
```

The scope is pinned to `default`, the one scope a Notion sign-in needs. Notion's 401 names it, but its metadata also
advertises `ema_issuer:manage`, its enterprise-managed auth scope, and OpenCode falls back to every advertised scope when
a challenge names none: the pin keeps that fallback from ever asking for more. A pinned `oauth.client_id` or
`oauth.redirect_uri` would be different, and wrong: either stops OpenCode signing in with its client metadata document,
`https://opencode.ai/oauth/opencode/client.json`, which Notion advertises that it accepts. So there is no client ID to
set and nothing is registered. Notion's server signs in with OAuth; no integration token or API key is used.

To change anything else, define `mcp.servers.notion` yourself at Notion's URL. The plugin then **adopts** your entry
unchanged, and `/notion-status` shows "Connection: connected (…, your own mcp.servers.notion, used unchanged)". Keep the
`"scope": "default"` it carries: an entry without a scope gets the fallback described above. The permission rules and
skills still apply. Of your entry the plugin reads only its type, its URL and whether `oauth` is
`false`; it never reads, copies or reports its `headers`.

### An MCP token, for a headless machine

A Business or Enterprise workspace owner can create an MCP token in Notion's developer portal (**New MCP token**), and a
client can send it as a bearer token with no browser sign-in. Keep it in an environment variable, never in the file:

```json
{
  "mcp": {
    "servers": {
      "notion": {
        "type": "remote",
        "url": "https://mcp.notion.com/mcp",
        "oauth": false,
        "headers": { "Authorization": "Bearer {env:NOTION_MCP_TOKEN}" }
      }
    }
  }
}
```

The plugin adopts that entry unchanged, and `/notion-status` names it "your own mcp.servers.notion without OAuth". There
is no `/connect` sign-in for it, and the plugin never reads the token. If it stops working, status's next step asks you
to check the token.

### A conflict

The plugin compares origin and path, so a trailing slash or a query string still matches. Any other URL, or a local
command, is a **conflict**: the plugin leaves your entry alone, adds nothing, status shows "Connection: conflict", and
gives the next step:

```text
- Next step: Your OpenCode config defines mcp.servers.notion with https://notion-mcp.example.com/mcp, but the plugin uses https://mcp.notion.com/mcp. Point it at https://mcp.notion.com/mcp or remove it, then restart OpenCode.
```

## Permissions

OpenCode asserts every MCP call itself, with the action `notion_<tool>` and the resource `*`. Notion's own tool names
start `notion-`, so each action is double-prefixed: `notion-search` becomes `notion_notion-search`. The plugin adds its
block to every agent that starts with the base rule `{ "action": "*", "resource": "*", "effect": "allow" }`, directly
after that rule. The README prints the whole block, rule for rule, in
[Permissions](https://github.com/joe-broadhead/opencode-notion/blob/HEAD/README.md#permissions); `/notion-status` prints
it too, and its `Agents without default rules` row prints it as a list to paste.

`READ_TOOLS` in `src/notion-tools.ts` lists Notion's read tools, `WRITE_TOOLS` its write tools, and `DESTRUCTIVE_TOOLS`
the nine that `access: "read-only"` denies and `access: "ask-changes"` asks for. A tool Notion adds later matches
`notion_*` alone, and takes the same value's effect. `/notion-status` names the tools in no list. A plan or an Enterprise
tool list can leave out tools the plugin knows, so a known tool missing from one connection is normal.

**Every tool is allowed by default**, so nothing is switched off for you. These deserve their own sentence before you
decide:

- `notion_notion-delete-pages`, `notion_notion-delete-databases` and `notion_notion-delete-comment` trash something
  everyone with access can see. Trash is recoverable only until the workspace's retention passes.
- `notion_notion-restore-version` replaces a whole page with a past version: every edit after that time is lost,
  including other people's, and the comments added since.
- `notion_notion-upload-skill` replaces a Skill page's title, Description, body and Files.
- `notion_notion-spawn-session`, `notion_notion-send-message-to-session` and `notion_notion-stop-session` drive a Notion
  Custom Agent that acts in the workspace with your permissions and spends AI credits.
- `notion_notion-calendar-cancel-events` removes an event from other people's calendars and may notify them.

There are three ways to restrict the block, and everything later still wins:

1. the `access` option, for the whole plugin;
2. the agent's own `permissions`, for one agent;
3. your top-level `permissions`, which OpenCode adds to every agent.

### `access`

| Value | What runs |
| --- | --- |
| `all` (the default) | every Notion tool runs without a prompt |
| `ask-changes` | a read runs; every other tool asks, including one Notion adds later |
| `read-only` | a read runs; every other tool is denied, and hidden from the model |

The value generates the block from the tool table's classes, so `/notion` and `/notion-status` always show what is in
force; the README prints the three blocks in full. A namespace rule (`notion_*`) comes first, and each known tool's own
rule after it, so a tool Notion adds later takes the value's own effect.

### Recipes

To restrict one agent, put the rules in that agent's own `permissions`; a top-level `ask` or `allow` would reach every
agent, Explore included. A read-only agent that asks for one change:

```json
{
  "agents": {
    "build": {
      "permissions": [
        { "action": "notion_*", "resource": "*", "effect": "ask" },
        { "action": "notion_notion-search", "resource": "*", "effect": "allow" },
        { "action": "notion_notion-fetch", "resource": "*", "effect": "allow" },
        { "action": "notion_notion-create-comment", "resource": "*", "effect": "ask" }
      ]
    }
  }
}
```

Never replace a whole page from OpenCode, in any agent (a `deny` also hides the tool):

```json
[{ "action": "notion_notion-update-page", "resource": "*", "effect": "deny" }]
```

**A permission rule matches a tool's name, not its arguments.** `notion_notion-update-page` is the routine change, and it
also carries the command that replaces a whole page's content. No rule can see that argument, so the guard is
`notion-write`: it never sends it unless the user asked to replace the whole page, and says in one line what will be
removed first. With `ask-changes` or `read-only` a rule cannot see it either, so read the input shown in the prompt
before you answer yes, or deny the tool as above.

Use only the rules you need. Never answer "Always allow" for a destructive tool: OpenCode would save an allow for every
agent in the project, and every later delete or whole-page restore would run unasked.

OpenCode uses the last rule that matches, so everything after the plugin's rules wins:

1. the agent's own rules, such as Explore's, which turn Notion off there;
2. your top-level `permissions`, which OpenCode adds to every agent;
3. your saved "Always allow" answers, which beat an `ask` but never a configured `deny`.

A `deny` on resource `*` also hides the tool from the model. In an unattended run such as `opencode run`, a tool that asks
is refused. An agent without the base rule gets no Notion rules and keeps its own behaviour.

### Agents that miss the rules

OpenCode creates agents that exist only in your config after plugins add their rules, so those agents get no Notion rules;
agents that a later plugin adds are in the same position. An agent counts as guarded when the plugin's whole block appears
anywhere after its base allow. Under `access: "all"` that changes nothing, because the block restates the base allow;
under `ask-changes` or `read-only`, `/notion-status` and `/notion` list every other agent that has a base allow and where
a new Notion tool would run unrestricted, by name, followed by the default rules to paste. The next step reads:

```text
Put the default rules shown by /notion-status first in each listed agent's own permissions, in opencode.json or the agent's Markdown file, followed by your top-level rules for Notion tools.
```

Put the block first in that agent's own `permissions`, then repeat after it any top-level rules you have for `notion_*`
tools, so yours keep winning. Never put the block in the top-level `permissions`: top-level rules come after every
agent's own rules, so it would loosen Explore. For an agent `reviewer`, with one top-level rule of your own:

```json
{
  "permissions": [{ "action": "notion_notion-delete-pages", "resource": "*", "effect": "deny" }],
  "agents": {
    "reviewer": {
      "description": "Reviews changes",
      "mode": "subagent",
      "permissions": [
        { "action": "notion_*", "resource": "*", "effect": "ask" },
        { "action": "notion_notion-search", "resource": "*", "effect": "allow" },
        { "action": "notion_notion-delete-pages", "resource": "*", "effect": "deny" }
      ]
    }
  }
}
```

Copy the full block from your own `/notion-status` output: the sample above keeps the first read allow and your own rule,
and leaves out the rest.

## Errors

Every error from the plugin reads `CODE: What happened. Next step: What to do.`

| Code | When | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `OPTIONS_INVALID` | Setup: an option is unknown or has a wrong value. `/plugins` shows the message, which names the option and the accepted values. | Fix the plugin options in `opencode.json`. |
| `HOST_UNTESTED` | Setup: OpenCode is outside `>=2.2.3 <2.3.0`, and `allowUntestedHost` is not set. | Use OpenCode `>=2.2.3 <2.3.0`, or set `"allowUntestedHost": true`. |
| `STATUS_UNAVAILABLE` | `/notion-status`, `/notion` or the status RPC: the status could not be read, or the plugin is not running on the server. The RPC answers with its error `unavailable`. | The message's own next step: restart OpenCode and run the command again, or, when the plugin is not running, run `/plugins` to see why. |
| `SKILLS_INVALID` | Setup: a skill file is missing or broken. The plugin still starts; status shows the problem. | Reinstall the plugin. |
| `SERVER_NOT_REGISTERED` | Setup: the `notion` server could not be registered. Status shows the problem. | Restart OpenCode. |
| `RULES_NOT_ADDED` | Setup: the default permission rules could not be added. Status shows the problem. | Restart OpenCode. |

For example:

```text
OPTIONS_INVALID: Unknown option "apiKey". Accepted options: "allowUntestedHost", "access". Next step: Fix the plugin options in opencode.json, for example "plugins": [{ "package": "github:joe-broadhead/opencode-notion#v0.0.1", "options": { "access": "ask-changes" } }].
```

Errors from Notion's server and from OpenCode pass through unchanged, except in the tools RPC for scripts, whose codes are
in [Scripting](scripting.md#errors). Notion's own errors name what happened: `validation_error`, whose
`additional_data.tool_error_code` can be `page_not_found` or `suggested_edit_stale`; `object_not_found`, which can mean no
access; `rate_limited`, with `retry_after_seconds` and `rate_limit_reason`; `service_overload`; and
`public_api_request_blocked`, which retrying will not change.

## Status and RPC

`/notion-status`, the `/notion` dialog and the RPC method `status` (RPC ID `notion.workspace`) share one status model. It
holds no token, no header and no URL query, and makes no Notion call. `version`, `host`, `state`, `unguardedAgents` and
`nextStep` are the fields every plugin of this family shares, with the same names and meanings:

| Field | Content |
| --- | --- |
| `version` | The plugin's version |
| `access` | The `access` value in force: `all`, `ask-changes` or `read-only`. |
| `state` | `connected`, `sign_in_required`, `connecting`, `disabled`, `failed`, `not_configured` or `conflict`. The `Connection` row shows the same states as `connected`, `sign-in required`, `connecting`, `disabled`, `failed`, `not configured` and `conflict`. |
| `error` | For a failed connection only: OpenCode's reason, on one line of at most 160 characters, with any URL cut before its query. The text for a needed sign-in can hold an authorization URL, so it is never shown. |
| `source` | `type` (`plugin`, `adopted` or `conflict`), `url`, `signIn` (`oauth`, or `own` for an entry with `"oauth": false`, such as an MCP token), and for a conflict the `expected` URL |
| `workspace` | The workspace's name from the last `notion-get-self` call since OpenCode started, or `null` before one. The plugin makes no call of its own. |
| `connection` | `person` for your own sign-in, `bot` for a workspace connection whose admin chose its tool list, or `null` before an account read. |
| `tools` | How many Notion tools OpenCode lists that the plugin knows; a tool Notion adds is counted under `unknownCount`. |
| `destructiveTools` | The listed tools of the destructive class. What happens to them follows `access`. `deniedTools` carries the same list under its old name. |
| `listing` | True while a server that connected moments ago lists no tools yet. The next step is then to run `/notion-status` again in a few seconds, not to ask an admin. |
| `unknownCount`, `unknownTools` | How many of them the plugin does not know, and at most 20 of their names, only those made of lowercase letters, digits, `_` and `-` |
| `unguardedAgents` | Agents where a new Notion tool would run unrestricted under `ask-changes` or `read-only`; always empty under `all`, where the block restates the base allow. An agent whose own rules already ask or deny for every Notion tool is not listed. |
| `shadowedSkills` | Present only when a skill with one of the plugin's ids, such as your own `notion` skill, replaces the plugin's: each `id` and the `path` OpenCode loads instead |
| `host` | `version` (`null` if OpenCode reports none), `range` (the supported range) and `tested` (true only for 2.2.3, 2.2.4, 2.2.5 and 2.2.6) |
| `problems` | Setup problems, each `CODE: What happened. Next step: What to do.` |
| `nextStep` | Exactly one next step: the `Next step` row, `Nothing to do.` when nothing is needed |

The `Access` row starts with the `access` value and the posture it gives, from the tool lists: "access all: every Notion
tool is allowed, reads and changes alike", or under `read-only`, "reads run without asking; the 29 writes and the 9
destructive tools are denied". Then it says whether that connection is a person's or a workspace connection's, when an
account read has said so, and whether those rules are in place: "every agent has the block", "default rules missing in
the agents listed below", or "default rules not added (see the OpenCode row)".

A sign-in that worked and then needed a new one adds a sentence to the next step: Notion revokes the whole grant when a
refresh token is reused, which two OpenCode processes sharing one sign-in do, so signing out and in again once is the fix.

When the status cannot be read, the method answers with its error `unavailable`: the message
`STATUS_UNAVAILABLE: Could not read Notion's status (…).` and `data: { nextStep }`.

# In Jelly

[Jelly](https://heyjelly.ai) runs OpenCode agents. It reads the `jelly` section of this
package's `package.json` as JSON, without loading the plugin, when a person reviews the exact
version, and uses it as follows.

Jelly names the plugin **Notion** (`jelly.title`), with the package name and version beneath. Under
that name it shows the one line in `jelly.summary`, and beside it the mark in `jelly.icon`
(`assets/icon.svg`, shipped in the package): Jelly reads that file once, when it records the
plugin, and keeps it only if it is a clean SVG of drawing elements, with no script, style, link
or outside reference. The mark is a neutral page with a folded corner on a slate tile, not
Notion's logo. Jelly's declaration contracts drop a top-level key they don't know, and refuse an
unknown key inside a tool, sign-in or `contributes` entry, so the section uses only the keys Jelly
reads.

## Icons and the vendor

`opencode.icons` lists the same mark in three files of this package, in order: `assets/icon.svg`, then
`assets/icon-128.png` and `assets/icon-256.png`, each a raster rendered from that SVG and each with its
MCP `mimeType` and exact `sizes`. `jelly.icon` stays `assets/icon.svg`, the same file as the first entry.
The three files are also exported as `./icon.svg`, `./icon-128.png` and `./icon-256.png`, so a consumer
can resolve them from the installed package, and all three are in the published tarball.

`opencode.vendor` names the service behind the plugin: `{ "id": "notion", "name": "Notion", "domain":
"notion.so" }`. A display app may show the vendor's official logo from the vendor's own site, under
the vendor's terms, using that domain. The package carries no vendor marks: every shipped file is this
family's own drawing, not Notion's logo, shape or brand colour.

## Tools and permissions

79 tools are declared (41 read-only), every tool in `src/notion-tools.ts`: each tool with `allow`, and only the reads
marked `readOnly`, which is what a read-only helper is allowed to run. Jelly's agents have no base "allow everything"
rule, so this plugin's own default rules, which it puts after that rule, never reach them; the declaration is the whole
posture. A declared `allow` changes nothing in Jelly, which already runs what Jelly's own settings permit.

Every declared tool is allowed, so nothing is switched off for you. These deserve their own sentence:

- The 29 writes, such as `notion_notion-update-page` (a property or content change everyone with access sees),
  `notion_notion-create-comment` (a comment, whose mention notifies someone) and `notion_notion-move-pages` (access can
  change with the new parent).
- The nine destructive tools: `notion_notion-delete-pages`, `notion_notion-delete-databases`,
  `notion_notion-delete-comment` (trash), `notion_notion-restore-version` (replaces a whole page),
  `notion_notion-upload-skill` (replaces a Skill page), `notion_notion-spawn-session`,
  `notion_notion-send-message-to-session`, `notion_notion-stop-session` (a Custom Agent) and
  `notion_notion-calendar-cancel-events` (an event others see).

A tool Notion adds later, a write included, is not declared, so in Jelly it runs with the plugin's own default: allowed,
even if it changes something such as a page's whole content, until a new version of this plugin declares it. Notion adds
tools over time, write actions included. A Jelly admin can set such a tool to ask. Keep `jelly.tools` in step with
`src/notion-tools.ts`; `test/unit/jelly.test.ts` checks the list against it, and each declared effect against the plugin's
own default rules.

## Skills

Declared: `notion`, `notion-write`. Jelly refuses an install whose skill ids collide with another plugin's or the agent's
own; they differ from the Google Workspace, Slack, Granola, Linear and Metaview plugins' skills, which share such
questions with them.

## Views

None: `jelly.views` and `jelly.rpc` are empty, and the plugin contributes no Home feed or widget. A feed of recent pages
would put workspace content on a dashboard and call Notion unasked.

## Signing in

`jelly.signIns` declares one sign-in, `notion`, for Notion's MCP server `notion`, which signs in with OpenCode's MCP OAuth.

Jelly folds the declared sign-in into this plugin's one card, which shows it as Connected, Not signed in or Sign in again

## Versions

Jelly's curated catalogue pins an exact version, so publish each release under a new version: a review in Jelly can then
tell the two apart.

# Scripting

A script can call Notion's tools with no model: a cron job, a shell script, or any program that can reach the OpenCode
server. It uses the tools RPC, `notion.workspace.tools`, through `opencode api` or an OpenCode client.

Every tool the plugin knows is a method, named after Notion's tool, without the `notion_` prefix. Each method carries a
class: the worst thing that tool can do.

| Class | Methods | What the class means |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `read` | one per known read: `notion-search`, `notion-fetch`, `notion-query-data-sources` and the others | it only reads |
| `write` | the twenty-three writes, such as `notion-update-page`, `notion-create-comment` and `notion-create-pages` | it changes what someone else can see, or notifies someone |
| `destructive` | `notion-calendar-cancel-events`, `notion-delete-comment`, `notion-delete-databases`, `notion-delete-pages`, `notion-restore-version`, `notion-send-message-to-session`, `notion-spawn-session`, `notion-stop-session`, `notion-upload-skill` | deletes or replaces a page, drives a Custom Agent, or cancels an event others see |
| `describe` | none: lists the methods, their class, their permission action, whether OpenCode lists each tool now, each tool's input as JSON Schema, and — given a session — whether that session may call it |

The methods keep Notion's hyphens, and in a URL they are plain path segments. The methods come from the plugin's one tool
table, `src/notion-tools.ts`: the known reads (`READ_TOOLS` in `src/notion-tools.ts`), the writes in `WRITE_TOOLS`, and
the destructive class in `DESTRUCTIVE_TOOLS`. Call `describe` for the list: a plan, or an Enterprise tool list, may leave
out a tool, and `describe` marks a known tool that Notion does not offer you as unavailable.

The class is never the decision: the rules are. A `write` and a `destructive` method are methods too, and they run
whenever the session's rules resolve them to `allow` — which the default `access: "all"` does, for every method. The
class decides what `access: "ask-changes"` and `"read-only"` restrict, and `describe` reports it beside the resolved
permission.

Results hold workspace content: keep what a script writes where the people it is about would expect it, and only as long
as you need it.

## A script runs as a session

Every call names a session, and the session must name an agent. The script runs as that agent, under the rules that
decide what its model sees: the agent's rules, then the session's, and the last rule that matches an action wins.

- **Only an `allow` runs.** The rules are resolved before anything is dispatched. An `ask` is refused with no prompt and
  no Notion call, because no one is there to answer it. A `deny` is refused with no Notion call.
- **A saved approval does not authorise a script.** An earlier "Always allow" is not part of the agent's and the
  session's rules, so a script that relied on one now needs an `allow` for its action in the session's or the agent's
  rules. This is deliberate; it keeps a script's grant reviewable rather than in a list of past clicks.
- **A script gets the same default.** Under `access: "all"` the block allows every method, so a script that names an
  agent with the default rules can call a read or a change with nothing more. Set `access: "ask-changes"` or
  `"read-only"`, or narrow the session's own rules, when a script should not change anything. An agent defined only in
  your config gets no default rules; `/notion-status` names it.

Create the session once, with the agent the script runs as, and keep its id. Give the project as the session's `location`: a session made without one belongs to the service's default location, where the project's agents may not exist, and each call then fails `Agent not found`. Never reuse a session found through history
or a list: the script would run as that session's agent, under its rules.

```sh
opencode api post /api/session -d '{"title":"weekly tracker","agent":"build","location":{"directory":"/path/to/project"}}'
```

Session rules come after the agent's, so a session can narrow what its script may do, or grant one action in a
narrowly written session. This one can search and fetch
pages, and nothing else in Notion:

```sh
opencode api post /api/session -d '{"title":"weekly tracker","agent":"build","location":{"directory":"/path/to/project"},"permissions":[
  {"action":"notion_*","resource":"*","effect":"deny"},
  {"action":"notion_notion-search","resource":"*","effect":"allow"},
  {"action":"notion_notion-fetch","resource":"*","effect":"allow"}
]}'
```

For a one-off script with an approval bound to it, use Jobs' `jobs_run_script`: the approval covers exactly that source
and that list of methods, and Jobs writes the run session's rules for you.

## Calling a method

The body is `{"input": {"sessionID": "<session>", "input": <the tool's input>}}`. Both keys are required, and no other
key is allowed.

```sh
opencode api post /api/rpc/notion.workspace.tools/notion-search -H "x-opencode-directory:$PWD" -d '{"input":{
  "sessionID":"ses_…",
  "input":{}
}}'
```

The tool's input is Notion's, and Notion defines its fields and may change them without notice: `describe` shows each
tool's schema as OpenCode lists it now. Check it rather than guess a field name or a filter's shape.

```sh
opencode api post /api/rpc/notion.workspace.tools/describe -H "x-opencode-directory:$PWD" -d '{"input":{}}'
opencode api post /api/rpc/notion.workspace.tools/describe -H "x-opencode-directory:$PWD" -d '{"input":{"sessionID":"ses_…"}}'
```

With a session, each method in the answer also carries `permission`: `allow`, `ask` or `deny`, resolved exactly as a call
would be. The answer also carries `location`, and `unclassified` when Notion lists a tool the plugin's table does not
classify. `SESSION_UNKNOWN` names the `x-opencode-directory` header, because a session created in one project is not
found from another.

A result comes back as `{ output?, text }`: the tool's structured content when it has any, and its text parts
joined by newlines. Notion content in it is untrusted data, written by other people, and a Notion AI summary is Notion
AI's.

## The location

Run the command in the project whose agent you mean, and send the call to that location explicitly:

```sh
opencode api post /api/rpc/notion.workspace.tools/<method> -H "x-opencode-directory:$PWD" -d '{…}'
```

Without it the call goes to the service's default location and fails `rpc.unavailable` if the plugin is not loaded
there. The HTTP equivalents are the `location[directory]` query parameter and the same header. `describe` reports the
`location` that answered and a `locationHint`.

A location unloads after OpenCode's idle timeout. If a scheduled script gets `rpc.unavailable` from a location that was
loaded before, send the call again once: the request loads the location. Jobs keeps its own location loaded.

## Rate limits

Every tool call counts against the workspace's request budget. A connection allows 180 requests a minute on Free, Plus and
Education, and 600 requests a minute on Business and Enterprise; a separate budget is shared across the whole workspace, so
a connection can be limited while under its own cap. Querying a data source has its own limit, about 3 requests a second.

Make calls one at a time, never in parallel. When Notion reports `rate_limited`, the method fails with `UPSTREAM_ERROR` and
the message carries `retry_after_seconds`: wait that long, then make fewer calls at once, and never retry in a loop. Notion
answers 429 or 529 with that body, and retries a rate limit once itself when the wait is two seconds or less.

A 503 (`service_overload`) on a write can mean the write was saved. Read the object before repeating it: never retry a
write that returned 503 before reading the object.

## Errors

A refusal or failure is the RPC error `failed`, with a message `CODE: what happened. Next step: what to do.` and
`data: { code, next }`. `opencode api` exits with status 1 for any RPC error, after printing the error's JSON to standard
output.

| Code | When |
| --- | --- |
| `SESSION_UNKNOWN` | OpenCode says the session does not exist in this location. The next step names the `x-opencode-directory` header. Any other failure to look the session up is OpenCode's own error. |
| `SESSION_AGENT_REQUIRED` | The session names no agent, or an agent that does not exist. |
| `PERMISSION_DENIED` | The last matching rule is an `ask` or a `deny`, so the call was refused before dispatch. An ask says that a script cannot answer and names the allow rule to add; a deny names the denied action, such as `notion_notion-search`, and says to remove or narrow that rule, add a later allow to the session, or use a session whose agent allows it. A saved "Always allow" does not help. |
| `SERVER_CONFLICT` | Your `opencode.json` defines its own `notion` server at a URL other than Notion's. `/notion-status` names both. |
| `AUTH_REQUIRED`, `CONNECTING`, `CONNECTION_FAILED`, `DISABLED`, `NOT_REGISTERED` | The `notion` server needs a sign-in, is still connecting, could not connect, is disabled, or is missing. `/notion-status` gives the details. |
| `TOOL_UNAVAILABLE` | The server is connected, but OpenCode does not list the tool: a plan or an Enterprise tool list may leave it out. |
| `UPSTREAM_ERROR` | Notion answered with an error, such as an invalid input, an object you cannot see or a rate limit. The message holds the first line of Notion's text, at most 300 characters, with tokens and URL query strings removed. |
| `CANCELLED` | The request was cancelled. |

OpenCode itself answers `rpc.method_not_found` for a method that does not exist, such as a tool Notion adds later, and
`rpc.invalid_input` for a body that is not the envelope above, with one message per problem:

| Problem | Message |
| --- | --- |
| The envelope is not an object | `the envelope must be an object, such as {"sessionID":"<session>","input":<the tool's input>}` |
| A key other than `sessionID` and `input` | `"extra" is not allowed`, naming the key |
| `sessionID` missing, not a string, or empty | `"sessionID" must be a non-empty string` |
| `input` missing | `"input" is missing` |
| `input` not an object | `"input" must be an object` |
| `describe` given anything but nothing, `{}` or `{"sessionID":"…"}` | `describe takes nothing, or {"sessionID":"<session>"}` |

## What scripts cannot do

- Run a method whose action resolves to `ask` or `deny`: no one can answer a prompt, and a deny needs its rule changed.
- Rely on a saved "Always allow" from the model path: a script needs an `allow` rule in config, or a Jobs one-off's
  approval.
- Call a tool that is not in the plugin's table, even with an allow rule. It is reported as `unclassified`.
- Delete, restore a whole page, upload a Skill, drive an agent or cancel an event without changing the deny first: the
  default rules refuse those nine.
- Use a token or key: the plugin has none to give.

A script's calls write nothing to the session, and OpenCode's `execute.before` and `execute.after` tool hooks, from any
plugin, do not run for them. The plugin applies the same result shaping it applies on the model path: a script's account
read fills the workspace and connection type for status, as the model's call does.
